remainingMisses.statement: She joined Duke University in 1994 as an assistant professor of pharmacology and cancer biology and had risen to full professor by 2005.
remainingMisses.explanation: missing: The dossier does not mention her joining Duke faculty, ranks, or dates 1994/2005.

remainingMisses.statement: Her research concerns cell growth and programmed cell death, including how cancer cells evade apoptosis and the role of caspase-2 in regulating the length of female fertility in vertebrates.
remainingMisses.explanation: partial: The dossier confirms general research focus but omits the specific detail regarding caspase-2 and female fertility.

remainingMisses.statement: At Duke she received a Research Mentoring award in 2012 and the Distinguished Faculty Award from the Duke Medical Alumni Association in 2013.
remainingMisses.explanation: missing: The dossier mentions election to the Institute of Medicine in 2013, but not the specific Research Mentoring or Distinguished Faculty Awards cited in the reference.

remainingMisses.statement: Throughout her presidency she has championed MIT's commitment to freedom of expression while maintaining that everyone remains free to do their best work.
remainingMisses.explanation: missing: The dossier does not mention her championing freedom of expression.

remainingMisses.statement: Bibliographic indexes record about 156 authored works and roughly 10,978 citations under her name.
remainingMisses.explanation: missing: The dossier does not mention specific citation counts or authored works.

remainingMisses.statement: In her 1 May 2023 inaugural address, Kornbluth described her own start as a hands-on cancer biologist — "pipette-and-centrifuge, buckets-and-buckets-of-frog-eggs" — running a laboratory of about twelve people doing curiosity-driven fundamental research into the cell biology and biochemistry that goes wrong when cells turn cancerous.
remainingMisses.explanation: missing: The dossier does not mention her inaugural address or specific quotes about her start as a biologist.

remainingMisses.statement: Posing the question "What are university leaders good for?", she answered from her own move into administration that leadership makes a difference by accelerating progress well beyond the narrow band of one’s own research.
remainingMisses.explanation: missing: The dossier does not mention her views on what university leaders are good for.

remainingMisses.statement: Kristalina Georgieva has served as the 12th Managing Director of the International Monetary Fund since 1 October 2019, the first person from an emerging market economy to lead the institution.
remainingMisses.explanation: partial: The dossier captures the 12th Managing Director role and the start year but lacks the specific date (October 1) and the claim of being the first from an emerging market economy.

remainingMisses.statement: She was Chief Executive of the World Bank Group from 2 January 2017 to 1 October 2019, a post established for her and abolished afterwards, and acting President of the World Bank Group from 1 February to 8 April 2019.
remainingMisses.explanation: partial: The dossier confirms the CEO role and rough timeframe but omits the acting President tenure and specific start/end dates.

remainingMisses.statement: As European Commissioner for Budget and Human Resources from 1 November 2014 to 31 December 2016 she managed the EU's budget and staff through the aftermath of the Eurozone debt crisis.
remainingMisses.explanation: partial: The title is stated but the specific tenure dates and the management of EU budget/staff during the crisis are not mentioned.

remainingMisses.statement: As European Commissioner for International Cooperation, Humanitarian Aid and Crisis Response from 2010 to 2014 she directed EU resources to people affected by crises including the 2010 Haiti earthquake.
remainingMisses.explanation: partial: The title is present but the specific dates, the directing of resources, and the Haiti earthquake event are missing.

remainingMisses.statement: She began her career by teaching economics.
remainingMisses.explanation: missing: No dossier statement addresses her career beginning in teaching economics.

remainingMisses.statement: Her BA, MA and PhD are all from the University of National and World Economy in Sofia.
remainingMisses.explanation: missing: No dossier statement mentions her education or degrees.

remainingMisses.statement: She succeeded Christine Lagarde at the IMF and Jim Yong Kim as acting World Bank president, and her IMF deputies have included David Lipton, Geoffrey Okamoto, Gita Gopinath and Dan Katz.
remainingMisses.explanation: missing: No dossier statement discusses who she succeeded or her IMF deputies.

remainingMisses.statement: The IMF's own biography page is not readable anonymously, so a reference built only from institutional pages would have nothing to say about her.
remainingMisses.explanation: missing: Recorded as a coverage note rather than a biographical fact: the IMF site answered anonymous collection with an access-denied page on 2026-09-06, so the self-reported account is unavailable to keyless research.

remainingMisses.statement: Asked how her crisis background applied to the pandemic downturn, Georgieva said five years as a crisis commissioner came in handy, gave her motto as "pray for the best, prepare for the worst, and act decisively", and observed that a crisis brings out both the worst and the best in people, citing solidarity she had seen after natural disaster and war.
remainingMisses.explanation: missing: No dossier statement covers her crisis motto or pandemic response remarks.

remainingMisses.statement: She contrasted IMF projections from three months earlier — 160 countries with positive income-per-capita growth — with the sudden reversal, stressing that uncertainty about the virus’s course and about vaccines and treatments made the outlook exceptionally hard for policymakers and people alike.
remainingMisses.explanation: missing: No dossier statement references IMF projections or the outlook reversal.
